extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, litigators, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to draft, construe, and evaluate patent specifications and claims — covering sufficiency of description, claim particularity, claim scope, product vs. process claims, multiplicity of claims, and identity/co-extensiveness of inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of specification (enablement/description)
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must "explain the invention itself, the manner of making it, and the mode of putting it in practice." Where an element of a new combination must have a certain form to operate and other known forms exist, the specification must say or show which known form is applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insufficient description that merely states an old element is part of the combination without specifying which known form applies renders the patent unavailable to the public without further experiments. Excessive description is not injurious unless introduced with fraudulent intention. (Illustrated by cases and authorities cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are inserted to conform to the statutory requirement that the patentee shall "particularly point out and distinctly claim the part, improvement, or combination which he claims as his invention." "The claims measure the invention."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A distinct and formal claim is necessary to ascertain the scope of the patented invention; a patent grants no exclusive right except to what is distinctly claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: What a claim covers (subject matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim covers and secures a process, a machine, a manufacture, a composition of matter, or a design, and never the function or result of either.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims may cover whole inventions or only parts/sub-processes/combinations. The specification may contain multiple claims for whole, parts, and sub-combinations; each claim must satisfy invention, novelty, and utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be definite so the public understands scope
rubrics_metrics.description: All claims are required to be definite, so that the public may know what they are prohibited from doing during the existence of the patent and what they are to have at the end of the term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree of particularity may be reached in various modes: e.g., a machine claim is sufficient if co-extensive with the machine; a part of a machine must be clearly indicated; combination claims should state constituent devices and use the word "combination."

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination claims may be result-oriented but raise fact issues
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may declare that it "covers so much of the described mechanism as effects a particular specified result," without specifying the parts themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such cases it is a question of fact for court determination which parts effect that result and are therefore covered by the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of alternatives in claims (e.g., "with or without")
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may combine alternatives by inserting words like "with or without" before the name or designation of one or more enumerated parts covered by the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historic example: the Charles Goodyear rubber patent claimed vulcanized India rubber "whether with or without other ingredients, chemically altered by the application of heat, substantially as described."

rubrics_metrics.name: Process and product must be separately claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: A process and its product, though securable by separate claims in one patent, cannot be covered by one claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A product having definite characteristics may be described and claimed by those characteristics independent of the process; but if a product claim is framed in terms of the process, nothing infringes it unless produced by that process. (Discussed via Plummer v. Sargent and related authorities.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Product claims framed by process language are limited to that process
rubrics_metrics.description: If a product claim is set forth in the terms of the process (e.g., "ornamented by the application of oil and heat, substantially as described"), then no product made otherwise will infringe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A product claim should describe product characteristics to avoid limiting the claim to a single process of manufacture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material-specific claims must specify the material
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an invention consists of an article made of a specific material, the claim must specify that material and will be void if it generalizes by words that cover materials useless for the purpose as well as the specific material described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use overly broad material language that sweeps in nonfunctional or useless materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims are independent and may vary in validity within one patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim is considered as setting forth a complete and independent invention; some claims in a specification may be valid while others are invalid for lack of particularity, invention, novelty, or utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If narrower claim adds an unpatentable element it is void; where possible, claims should be construed to differ rather than to be identical because applicants normally would not repeat the same claim unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Needless multiplication of nebulous claims is void
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters patent that contain a needless multiplication of nebulous claims calculated to mislead the public are void for that reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plural claims that cover the same thing are not void merely for plurality unless there is evidence of intent to mislead; surplus claims without such intent may be dismissed as redundant.

rubrics_metrics.name: If all claims are void the patent is void
rubrics_metrics.description: If all the claims of a patent are void (for want of particularity, invention, novelty, utility, or other reason), the patent itself is void, even though valid claims might have been supported by the descriptive part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invalidity is a legal inference from failure to give statutory particularity, not dependent on inventor's intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims broader than the described invention are void
rubrics_metrics.description: Any claim which is broader than the described invention is void, even where the described invention is valuable and could have supported a valuable claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must be co-extensive with what is described and intended to be secured; overbroad claiming is fatal to those claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical hierarchy: class, order, genus, species, variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions are divisible into classes, orders, genuses, species, and varieties; every invention belongs to a variety, species, genus, etc., whether or not it is the first in that group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent that stands at the head of its genus may properly have a generic claim and a specific claim; Patent Office practice requires a separate application for each species for separate patents but allows generic claims appropriately placed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory particularity is jurisdictional for Commissioner authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory requirements relevant to particularity in descriptions and claims are conditions precedent to the Commissioner's authority to issue letters patent; if issued without conformity, the document is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invalidity of issued patents on inadequate specifications cannot be cured by showing the inadequacy arose from ignorance rather than fraud. Insufficient specification is a defence available by special plea or under equity rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity of specification to statutory requirements is a fact question
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the specification and claims conform to statutory particularity requirements is a question of fact for a jury in law actions or for a chancellor in equity; it is a question of evidence, not of construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will assess factual evidence to determine adequacy rather than resolving it as a pure construction issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Related vs unrelated inventions in one patent application
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent which describes and separately claims two or more related inventions is not void for that reason; if unrelated inventions are combined, the patent might be held invalid (though this has rarely been done).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether inventions are so related as to be combined in one application is a question of fact (Steinmetz v. Allen). Patent Office rules cannot arbitrarily prohibit combining related inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple patents for different parts of one extensive machine permissible
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more related patents may lawfully be granted for different parts of one extensive machine; in such cases the whole machine should be described and pictured in each specification so the patents differ only in their claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, plurality of patents cannot be granted for different uses of the same invention; all uses inherent in or described as part of the invention are covered by a single patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only one valid original patent per inventor per invention; identity determined by claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Only one valid original patent can be granted to an inventor on one invention; when multiple similar original patents exist, identity or non-identity is determined by comparing the claims and finding whether they are co-extensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are co-extensive if they cover the same combination (same number, same parts, same features). Claims specifying different combinations or omitting features are not co-extensive. The order of applications (dates) controls in determining junior vs senior rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction principle: claims control; cannot read-in unclaimed elements
rubrics_metrics.description: To construe letters patent is to determine precisely what inventions they cover; nothing described is secured unless covered by a claim, and no element not mentioned in a claim can be read into it even if it appears in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim narrower than the actual invention cannot be broadened by construction; a claim broader than permitted by the state of the art cannot be narrowed by construction contrary to its language. Newly discovered uses not indicated in the patent cannot affect claim construction. Construction depends on the claims and established claim-construction rules.
